lead: A digital image system is not one program but a chain. Light from a scene reaches a sensor, the sensor's charge becomes numbers, and those numbers pass through a series of jobs: cleaned, sharpened, compressed, cut into objects, described, matched to a name. Each job has a physical home — a camera, a cable, a processor, a disk, a screen. So every first unit looks at the same system twice: the blocks you can point at, and the steps you can name. Both views let you place a new algorithm on the chain instead of treating it as an isolated trick.
prereq: You need: 1.1 Origins and applications for why the chain exists, and 1.4 Light, image sensing and acquisition for what happens inside the first block.

sections.h3: The functional chain: nine jobs from photons to a label

blocks.text: Look at any image system and ask two questions. What blocks does the signal pass through? What job does each block do? The first question gives physical components. The second gives functional steps, which some syllabi call the fundamental steps in digital image processing.

Acquisition turns scene energy into numbers: a lens and a sensor give a continuous signal, and a digitizer samples it on a grid and quantizes each sample to an integer. Preprocessing is the cheap cleaning done before any clever step — rescale intensities, remove a fixed sensor pattern, flatten uneven lighting.

Enhancement makes the picture look better to a human eye, such as brightening a night photo of a Chennai street. A viewer judges it, so two viewers may disagree. Restoration undoes a known damage — hand shake, motion blur, sensor noise. It needs a model of how the damage was made, and that model is the difference from enhancement.

Color processing works in a color space: correct a colour cast, or map a grey X-ray to false colour. Compression spends fewer bits on the same picture, so it sits before storage or transmission, not after. Segmentation cuts the image into parts — road, number plate, person. Representation and description turn a part into numbers: a boundary as a chain code, a region as its area and centroid. Recognition attaches the name: this region is a number plate.

items: Low level: image in, image out — acquisition, preprocessing, enhancement, restoration, color, compression.
Mid level: image in, attributes out — segmentation, representation.
High level: attributes in, decision out — recognition.
Not every system runs all nine. A barcode reader runs acquisition, threshold, decode.

sections.h3: Physical components: the hardware behind each step

head: Component
Job
rows: The scene and the light falling on it
Converts light energy into a continuous electrical signal
Samples the signal on a grid and quantizes values to integers
Runs the steps — CPU, GPU or DSP
Frame buffer for the current frame, disk for the archive
Moves frames between camera, server and phone

blocks.text: The frame buffer must hold at least one full frame. For a 2048×2048 sensor at 12 bits per pixel that is 2048×2048×12 = 50,331,648 bits, about 6 MiB — the number worked out in the example below. A phone that scans a UPI QR code holds one small frame in the buffer, runs thresholding and decoding on the processor, and never writes to disk.

The sensor is not the digitizer. The sensor outputs a continuous voltage; the digitizer decides where to sample and how many brightness levels exist. Those two choices are resolution, and they are the subject of 1.6 Sampling and quantization.

sections.h3: Feedback: the chain is not one-way

blocks.text: The arrows in the figure can point back. If recognition keeps rejecting a region, the split was wrong, so you return to segmentation with a different threshold. If enhancement exposes noise that was invisible before, you return to restoration, or to acquisition for a longer exposure. If the compressed file misses its bit budget, you return to enhancement and soften it. Drawing these return arrows is correct engineering, not a mistake.

Some orders are fixed by purpose. Compression must come before storage or transmission, because its whole job is to save bits there. Representation must come before recognition, because a classifier compares numbers, not pixels. Color processing sits before compression in the figure because a colour transform is often the first stage of the compressor itself.

One order is a convention. Restoration and enhancement are both preparation; some books put restoration first because a degradation model is known and objective, while enhancement is judged by eye. Follow whichever order your syllabus draws and say why.

figure.caption: Nine jobs in order: segmentation is where pixels become objects, recognition where an object gets its name. One raw frame here is 2048×2048×12 bits = 6 MiB, so compression comes before the disk or the network — and the dashed arrow back shows the usual feedback, re-splitting when recognition rejects a region.

spec.title: Functional chain: 9 steps
spec.aria: A top-to-bottom chain runs acquisition, preprocessing, enhancement, restoration, color processing, compression, segmentation, representation and recognition in that order, with a dashed feedback arrow from recognition back to segmentation.

examples.question: A machine-vision camera has a 2048×2048 pixel sensor and stores 12 bits per pixel. Raw frames go to a 4 GiB pen drive (sold as 4 GB). Ignoring file headers, find (a) the bits and bytes in one raw frame, (b) how many whole frames fit on the drive, and (c) where compression sits in the functional chain.
steps: Whole frames = 4096 ÷ 6 = 682.67, so 682 frames; 682 × 6 = 4092 MiB used, 4 MiB left over.
Compression sits after enhancement and restoration and before storage or transmission, since its purpose is to save bits exactly there.
examples.answer: One frame is 50,331,648 bits = 6,291,456 bytes = 6 MiB, 682 whole frames fit on the 4 GiB drive, and compression sits after enhancement/restoration and before storage or transmission.
examples.check:
w, h, bpp = 2048, 2048, 12
px = w * h
bits = px * bpp
byts = bits // 8
mib = byts / (1024 * 1024)
drive_mib = 4 * 1024
frames = int(drive_mib // mib)
for v in (px, bits, byts, mib, drive_mib, frames):
    print(v)

traps: Calling segmentation a low-level preprocessing step. It is mid-level: image in, attributes out. Thresholding a noisy night frame on raw intensities splits on noise, not on objects.
Putting compression before enhancement or restoration. You compress the picture you intend to keep; compressing earlier discards detail no later step can bring back.
Mixing up enhancement and restoration. Enhancement is subjective and needs no model; restoration is objective and needs a degradation model. Examiners love this pair.
Saying the sensor and the digitizer are the same block. The sensor gives a continuous signal; the digitizer (ADC) samples and quantizes it.
Drawing the chain as strictly one-way. Feedback from recognition back to segmentation, or from enhancement back to acquisition, is allowed and often expected.

quiz.q: List the nine functional steps of a digital image processing system in order.
quiz.a: Acquisition, preprocessing, enhancement, restoration, color processing, compression, segmentation, representation (with description), recognition.

quiz.q: Why does compression come after enhancement and restoration, not before?
quiz.a: Compression reduces the bits used to store or send an image. You compress the picture you intend to keep, so the steps that settle the final picture must run first. Compressing earlierthrows away detail that no later step can recover.

quiz.q: A frame buffer holds 1024×1024 pixels at 8 bits per pixel. How many such frames fit in 512 MiB?
How many bytes does one uncompressed 1920×1080 frame take at 24 bits per pixel?
Why must representation come before recognition?
quiz.a: Recognition compares an object against stored patterns, and a comparison needs numbers. Representation reduces a region or boundary to a short vector — chain code, area, centroid — and recognition then labels that vector.

quiz.q: Name four physical components of an image processing system and give the job of each in one line.
quiz.a: Sensor: light to a continuous electrical signal. Digitizer: samples and quantizes to integers. Processor: runs the functional steps. Memory: frame buffer plus archive. Display: shows the result. Any four.

quiz.q: A designer places segmentation right after acquisition, before enhancement, on night-time traffic video. What goes wrong?
quiz.a: Night frames are dark and noisy, so a threshold on raw intensities follows noise rather than vehicles. Enhancement, or restoration of sensor noise, must run first to raise contrast. Segmentation is mid-level and expects a usable image, not a raw one.

quiz.q: Give two places where a feedback arrow is useful, and what triggers it.
quiz.a: Recognition back to segmentation when the classifier keeps rejecting a region — the split is wrong, so re-segment with a new threshold. Enhancement back to acquisition or restoration when brightening exposes noise that was hidden — take a longer exposure or denoise first. Compression back to enhancement when the bit budget is missed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Every phone camera already runs a hardware version of this chain inside its image signal processor: the Bayer sensor output is demosaiced, denoised, colour-corrected, sharpened and JPEG-compressed before your app sees a single pixel. Cloud vision services split the chain across two machines, with compression and communication in between. Modern project teams call the same diagram an inference pipeline and measure latency at every block. Search "image signal processing pipeline" and "vision inference pipeline" to see the industry block diagrams.
